VLANs and Trunking Deep Dive

Why VLANs matter: isolation, performance, and flexible management for enterprise networks.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Verification & Troubleshooting
screens.narratorSegment: Learning objectives extend beyond configuration to verification and troubleshooting so you can detect and correct common errors quickly. You will learn the key show commands on Juniper EX Series switches that confirm VLAN definitions, interface modes, and routing state. For example, show vlans lists each VLAN name, ID, and whether it has an associated IRB interface. show interfaces terse or show interfaces ge-0/0/2 detail helps determine whether a port is in access or trunk mode and whether frames are being tagged. show route confirms that IRB interfaces are present as next hops for inter‑VLAN traffic. Each verification skill reduces mean time to repair and prevents silent segmentation failures in production.

screens.title: What is a VLAN?
screens.narratorSegment: A VLAN is a logical broadcast domain inside a physical switch fabric. In plain terms, it lets you group devices that should see each other's broadcasts and be on the same subnet, even if their ports are physically scattered. The switch achieves this separation by tagging Ethernet frames with a VLAN identifier according to the 802.1Q standard. That tag is how network devices know which logical segment a frame belongs to as it traverses the switching infrastructure. A concrete example: put HR desktops and HR servers in VLAN 10 so broadcasts for address resolution stay within that group and don't flood Sales or Guest devices. A common misconception is to treat VLANs as security boundaries on their own — they isolate broadcasts, but they do not encrypt or filter traffic between VLANs. For enforced separation, pair VLANs with access control lists or routing policies. Another practical point: VLAN IDs are numeric and limited by 802.1Q to 12 bits, giving 4096 values with two reserved IDs. When designing VLANs, choose clear naming and consistent ID assignment and document them. Key takeaway: VLANs control broadcast domains; they are the building blocks of network segmentation but must be paired with routing and policy to implement security.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › What is a VLAN?
VLAN — a compact definition

A VLAN is a logical broadcast domain created by tagging frames with a VLAN ID. It groups devices that should share layer 2 connectivity without regard to physical port location.

Key points
  • Logical separation, not encryption or routing by itself.
  • 802.1Q adds a 4-byte tag containing VLAN ID to identify the segment.
  • VLANs reduce broadcast domains and aid traffic management.
Analogy
Think of VLANs as separate rooms in the same building: people in one room hear each other but not those in another room unless a door (router) is opened.
Example
HR VLAN 10
All HR desktops and servers are in VLAN 10. Broadcasts such as ARP requests stay inside VLAN 10. To reach other VLANs, HR uses an IRB gateway IP.
Common misconception
VLANs are not security boundaries by themselves. Without routing policies or ACLs, devices from other VLANs can communicate if routing allows it.
Key Takeaway

Use VLANs to segment broadcast domains; pair them with routing and policy to enforce access control.

screens.title: 802.1Q Tagging and VLAN ID Range
screens.narratorSegment: IEEE 802.1Q defines how VLAN identity is carried inside Ethernet frames. The standard inserts a 4-byte tag into the frame header that contains a 12-bit VLAN identifier, allowing up to 4096 VLAN values. In practice, two IDs are reserved by the standard and operating systems, leaving 4094 usable IDs for administrators. You will rarely use all possible IDs; consistent numbering and clear naming are more important for operations. For example, choose contiguous ranges for department VLANs: 10–19 for ADMIN, 20–29 for GUEST, and so on. A common pitfall is relying on default VLAN 1 for production traffic; many teams change the native VLAN to an unused ID to reduce accidental exposure and VLAN hopping risks. Remember that tagging is only applied on trunk links. When a frame exits an access port the switch strips the 802.1Q tag, so end devices see untagged frames as usual. Practical planning means documenting VLAN IDs and ensuring trunk links allow the expected range of VLANs. When you see unexpected traffic on a VLAN, verify tag handling and numbering across all switches in the path.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › 802.1Q Tagging
The 4-byte tag and VLAN ID range

802.1Q adds a 4-byte field into the Ethernet header. That field contains a 12-bit VLAN ID. Numerically, this gives 0–4095 values; two are reserved and not used for normal VLANs.

Practical ID planning
  • Pick contiguous ranges per function (e.g., 10–19 Admin, 20–29 Guest).
  • Avoid using VLAN 1 for native traffic on trunks.
  • Document name↔ID mappings in your runbook.
Access vs trunk behavior
Access ports carry untagged frames for a single VLAN; trunks carry tagged frames for multiple VLANs. Untagged traffic on a trunk is mapped to the native VLAN.
Misconception
Some assume 4096 usable VLANs; remember the reserved IDs and platform-specific restrictions that may reduce usable space.
Key Takeaway

Tagging identifies VLANs across trunks; pick clear IDs, avoid default native VLANs, and keep the plan consistent across switches.

screens.title: Access Port vs Trunk Port
screens.narratorSegment: Access and trunk ports are the fundamental port modes you will configure. An access port is assigned to a single VLAN and is intended for end devices like workstations or printers. When a frame leaves an access port, the switch removes any VLAN tag so the endpoint receives a standard untagged Ethernet frame. Conversely, a trunk port carries traffic for multiple VLANs across a single physical link. Trunking relies on 802.1Q tags to distinguish frames belonging to different VLANs. A concrete example: configure a server-facing port as an access port in VLAN 10, while the uplink between two switches is a trunk that allows VLANs 10 and 20. A common misconfiguration is setting the wrong port-mode on an uplink — if you accidentally configure an uplink as an access port, one of your VLANs will be cut off from the other switch. Another frequent issue is assigning multiple VLANs to an access port; that will not work because access mode accepts only one VLAN. Understanding these behaviors prevents connectivity surprises in multi-switch topologies. Access Port vs Trunk Port means access ports map a single vlan to end devices; trunk ports carry many vlans tagged with 802.1q between network devices.. In practical terms, when to use each and how frames are handled. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Access Port vs Trunk Port
Access Port

Designed for a single VLAN. Frames entering are implicitly assigned to the configured VLAN. Frames exiting are untagged so end hosts see normal Ethernet frames.

When to use
  • Workstations, printers, servers connecting to a single VLAN.
  • When endpoints cannot handle tagged frames.
Trunk Port

Carries multiple VLANs using 802.1Q tags. Used between switches or to routers so many VLANs can traverse a single physical link.

When to use
  • Uplinks between switches and switch-to-router links for multiple VLANs.
  • When bandwidth consolidation is desirable across VLANs.
Example
ge-0/0/0 — access
set interfaces ge-0/0/0 unit 0 family ethernet-switching vlan members ADMIN
ge-0/0/1 — trunk
set interfaces ge-0/0/1 unit 0 family ethernet-switching port-mode trunk set interfaces ge-0/0/1 unit 0 family ethernet-switching vlan members [ADMIN GUEST]

screens.title: Configure VLANs on Juniper EX Series
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through the exact Junos commands for defining VLANs and assigning them to interfaces. Start by creating the named VLAN and assigning it an ID with set vlans NAME vlan-id ID. For example, set vlans ADMIN vlan-id 10 creates a logical segment called ADMIN with VLAN ID 10. Next, attach an access port by assigning the VLAN name to the interface's ethernet-switching family. For instance, set interfaces ge-0/0/0 unit 0 family ethernet-switching vlan members ADMIN makes ge-0/0/0 an access port for that VLAN. A common error is to assign an interface to a VLAN before creating the VLAN globally; the switch accepts the assignment but will not handle traffic correctly until the VLAN ID exists. After configuration, always run show vlans to confirm the vlan-id is present and show interfaces terse to ensure the interface is in ethernet-switching mode. In practice, script these changes or apply them in a configuration session with commit confirmation on production switches. This ensures you avoid partial changes that break host connectivity. The visible code block shows both creation and an access assignment example you can adapt for your topology.

keyIdea.text: Create the VLAN globally with an ID, then assign interfaces to it under family ethernet-switching; verify with show vlans and show interfaces.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Configure VLANs on Juniper EX
Step-by-step commands
# Create VLANs
set vlans ADMIN vlan-id 10
set vlans GUEST vlan-id 20

# Assign access port for ADMIN
set interfaces ge-0/0/0 unit 0 family ethernet-switching vlan members ADMIN

# Assign access port for GUEST
set interfaces ge-0/0/1 unit 0 family ethernet-switching vlan members GUEST

commit and-quit
After committing, verify with show vlans and show interfaces terse to confirm vlan-ids and port modes are active.
Validation checklist
  • Does show vlans list the new VLAN name and vlan-id?
  • Is the interface in ethernet-switching family per show interfaces?
  • Do hosts in the VLAN receive expected DHCP leases and can they ARP the gateway?
Key Takeaway

Define VLANs first, then assign ports; confirm with show commands to avoid orphaned interface assignments.

screens.title: Configure Trunk Ports and Native VLAN
screens.narratorSegment: Configuring trunk ports on Juniper EX switches involves three main steps: set the port to trunk mode, specify which VLANs traverse the trunk, and set the native VLAN if you want to change the default. Use set interfaces INTERFACE unit 0 family ethernet-switching port-mode trunk to enable trunking. Then add set interfaces INTERFACE unit 0 family ethernet-switching vlan members [LIST] to list the VLANs that should flow across the link. Finally, configure set interfaces INTERFACE unit 0 family ethernet-switching native-vlan-id ID to change the untagged VLAN on the trunk. A common security best practice is to choose an unused native VLAN ID (for example 999) instead of leaving VLAN 1 as native. The reason is that untagged traffic arriving on a trunk will be mapped to the native VLAN; mismatched native VLANs between two ends can cause untagged frames to be incorrectly assigned, leading to traffic leakage or VLAN hopping risk. After applying these commands, verify both sides of the trunk have matching allowed VLAN lists and the same native VLAN ID to avoid asymmetric behavior. Configure Trunk Ports and Native VLAN means trunk ports carry multiple vlans using tags; set a consistent native vlan on both ends and limit allowed vlans to what you need.. In practical terms, setting port-mode trunk, allowed vlans, and a secure native vlan. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Trunk essentials
keyIdea.text: Trunk ports carry multiple VLANs using tags; set a consistent native VLAN on both ends and limit allowed VLANs to what you need.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Configure Trunk Ports
Trunk configuration example
# Set port to trunk
set interfaces ge-0/0/2 unit 0 family ethernet-switching port-mode trunk

# Allow specific VLANs across the trunk
set interfaces ge-0/0/2 unit 0 family ethernet-switching vlan members [ADMIN GUEST]

# Set a secure native VLAN
set interfaces ge-0/0/2 unit 0 family ethernet-switching native-vlan-id 999

commit and-quit
Check that both ends of the trunk have identical allowed VLANs and the same native VLAN to avoid misrouting untagged frames.
Why change native VLAN?
Default native VLANs can be exploited in VLAN hopping attacks. Using an unused native VLAN and keeping it consistent across trunks reduces this risk and prevents accidental untagged traffic mapping to a sensitive production VLAN.
Misconfiguration symptom
If two switches have mismatched native VLANs, untagged traffic may be assigned to different VLANs at each end, producing odd connectivity and security gaps.

screens.title: Inter‑VLAN Routing with IRB
screens.narratorSegment: Inter-VLAN routing is required when devices in different VLANs need to communicate. On a Layer 3 switch this is accomplished with Integrated Routing and Bridging interfaces, known as IRB. An IRB interface is a logical interface that holds an IP address and represents the Layer 3 gateway for a specific VLAN. For example, configuring irb.10 with address 192.168.10.1/24 and associating it to VLAN 10 makes that IP the default gateway for devices in VLAN 10. The typical workflow is twofold: create the irb unit and assign the IP, then bind the VLAN's l3-interface to that irb unit using set vlans NAME l3-interface irb. X. A common operational tip is to keep the irb unit number aligned with the VLAN ID to simplify management. A frequent misconception is that an IRB automatically exposes ACLs between VLANs; routing happens by default, so apply firewall filters or policies if you want to restrict traffic between VLANs. Always verify routes and local interface entries with show route and show interfaces terse after configuration. Inter‑VLAN Routing with IRB means irb interfaces serve as per‑vlan gateways on layer 3 switches; bind them to vlans so traffic between vlans is routed by the switch.. In practical terms, how integrated routing and bridging provides gateways for vlans. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Common Mistakes and How to Diagnose Them
screens.narratorSegment: In practice, three misconfigurations recur: missing global VLAN definitions, incorrect port mode, and native VLAN mismatches. First, assigning an interface to a VLAN name without creating that VLAN with a vlan-id means the switch has an orphaned assignment; hosts won't be able to reach DHCP or peers in that VLAN. If a host cannot get a DHCP lease, confirm set vlans NAME vlan-id ID exists. Second, configuring an uplink as an access port by mistake isolates the VLAN on that link; this often appears as a whole VLAN unreachable beyond one switch. Check show interfaces terse to verify port-mode. Third, native VLAN mismatches on trunks map untagged frames to different VLANs across the link, producing surprising reachability and a security window. The symptom is traffic arriving in an unexpected VLAN at the remote end. Diagnose this with show interfaces interface-name to confirm native-vlan-id on both sides and align them. Always use show vlans and show route as part of diagnosis. When you find a mismatch, fix configuration and re-verify; sometimes rebooting edge devices is unnecessary if the switch corrects the VLAN mappings immediately.

fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter we explore VLANs beyond the basics so you can design and operate secure, segmented enterprise networks. You will learn how IEEE 802.1Q tags carry VLAN identity, how access and trunk ports behave differently, and how a Layer 3 switch uses Integrated Routing and Bridging interfaces to route between VLANs. We'll use Juniper EX Series commands to create VLANs, assign ports, configure trunking with a secure native VLAN, and attach IRB interfaces as gateways. Along the way I'll show common misconfigurations—like missing global VLAN definitions or native-VLAN mismatches—and how they produce surprising behavior. By the end, you will understand both the syntax to make changes and the reasoning for those choices: which interfaces become access-only, how trunk links aggregate multiple VLANs, and where routing must occur to enable cross‑VLAN communication. A concrete scenario in this chapter configures ADMIN and GUEST VLANs across two switches with a trunk and IRB routing, and we'll verify connectivity. Think of this as the operational checklist you will use when segmenting an enterprise floor or connecting multiple distribution switches: define VLANs, set port modes, secure the native VLAN, and expose IRB gateways carefully.

These four objectives focus your practice and verification steps so you can operate VLANs and trunks with confidence. First, you will explain why VLANs exist and how logical segmentation reduces broadcast domains and improves security. To make that concrete, you should be able to describe a scenario where HR and Guest networks live on separate VLANs but share a single physical switch. Second, you will configure and verify advanced VLAN assignments on Juniper EX switches: creating named VLANs, setting vlan-id, and confirming membership with verification commands. Third, you will implement and troubleshoot 802.1Q trunking, including setting port-mode trunk, defining the permitted VLAN list, and configuring a safe native VLAN. A practical example is configuring a trunk between two switches that carries HR and GUEST networks while using an unused native VLAN for security. Fourth, you will describe and set up inter‑VLAN routing with IRB interfaces on a Layer 3 switch so that each VLAN has a gateway IP and can reach other VLANs when appropriate. Each objective includes verification steps so you can confirm correct operation and catch common mistakes quickly.

Learning objectives extend beyond configuration to verification and troubleshooting so you can detect and correct common errors quickly. You will learn the key show commands on Juniper EX Series switches that confirm VLAN definitions, interface modes, and routing state. For example, show vlans lists each VLAN name, ID, and whether it has an associated IRB interface. show interfaces terse or show interfaces ge-0/0/2 detail helps determine whether a port is in access or trunk mode and whether frames are being tagged. show route confirms that IRB interfaces are present as next hops for inter‑VLAN traffic. This objective also teaches how to reason about symptoms: if a host on an access port cannot obtain DHCP, check that the VLAN exists globally and that the access port is assigned to it. If two switches cannot pass traffic for a VLAN, check allowed VLAN lists and native VLAN consistency on trunks. Each verification skill reduces mean time to repair and prevents silent segmentation failures in production.

A VLAN is a logical broadcast domain inside a physical switch fabric. In plain terms, it lets you group devices that should see each other's broadcasts and be on the same subnet, even if their ports are physically scattered. The switch achieves this separation by tagging Ethernet frames with a VLAN identifier according to the 802.1Q standard. That tag is how network devices know which logical segment a frame belongs to as it traverses the switching infrastructure. A concrete example: put HR desktops and HR servers in VLAN 10 so broadcasts for address resolution stay within that group and don't flood Sales or Guest devices. A common misconception is to treat VLANs as security boundaries on their own — they isolate broadcasts, but they do not encrypt or filter traffic between VLANs. For enforced separation, pair VLANs with access control lists or routing policies. Another practical point: VLAN IDs are numeric and limited by 802.1Q to 12 bits, giving 4096 values with two reserved IDs. When designing VLANs, choose clear naming and consistent ID assignment and document them. Key takeaway: VLANs control broadcast domains; they are the building blocks of network segmentation but must be paired with routing and policy to implement security.

IEEE 802.1Q defines how VLAN identity is carried inside Ethernet frames. The standard inserts a 4-byte tag into the frame header that contains a 12-bit VLAN identifier, allowing up to 4096 VLAN values. In practice, two IDs are reserved by the standard and operating systems, leaving 4094 usable IDs for administrators. You will rarely use all possible IDs; consistent numbering and clear naming are more important for operations. For example, choose contiguous ranges for department VLANs: 10–19 for ADMIN, 20–29 for GUEST, and so on. A common pitfall is relying on default VLAN 1 for production traffic; many teams change the native VLAN to an unused ID to reduce accidental exposure and VLAN hopping risks. Remember that tagging is only applied on trunk links. When a frame exits an access port the switch strips the 802.1Q tag, so end devices see untagged frames as usual. Practical planning means documenting VLAN IDs and ensuring trunk links allow the expected range of VLANs. When you see unexpected traffic on a VLAN, verify tag handling and numbering across all switches in the path.

Access and trunk ports are the fundamental port modes you will configure. An access port is assigned to a single VLAN and is intended for end devices like workstations or printers. When a frame leaves an access port, the switch removes any VLAN tag so the endpoint receives a standard untagged Ethernet frame. Conversely, a trunk port carries traffic for multiple VLANs across a single physical link. Trunking relies on 802.1Q tags to distinguish frames belonging to different VLANs. A concrete example: configure a server-facing port as an access port in VLAN 10, while the uplink between two switches is a trunk that allows VLANs 10 and 20. A common misconfiguration is setting the wrong port-mode on an uplink — if you accidentally configure an uplink as an access port, one of your VLANs will be cut off from the other switch. Another frequent issue is assigning multiple VLANs to an access port; that will not work because access mode accepts only one VLAN. Understanding these behaviors prevents connectivity surprises in multi-switch topologies. Access Port vs Trunk Port means access ports map a single vlan to end devices; trunk ports carry many vlans tagged with 802.1q between network devices.. In practical terms, when to use each and how frames are handled. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. Let's walk through the exact Junos commands for defining VLANs and assigning them to interfaces. Start by creating the named VLAN and assigning it an ID with set vlans NAME vlan-id ID. Configuring trunk ports on Juniper EX switches involves three main steps: set the port to trunk mode, specify which VLANs traverse the trunk, and set the native VLAN if you want to change the default. Use set interfaces INTERFACE unit 0 family ethernet-switching port-mode trunk to enable trunking. Then add set interfaces INTERFACE unit 0 family ethernet-switching vlan members [LIST] to list the VLANs that should flow across the link. Finally, configure set interfaces INTERFACE unit 0 family ethernet-switching native-vlan-id ID to change the untagged VLAN on the trunk. A common security best practice is to choose an unused native VLAN ID (for example 999) instead of leaving VLAN 1 as native. The reason is that untagged traffic arriving on a trunk will be mapped to the native VLAN; mismatched native VLANs between two ends can cause untagged frames to be incorrectly assigned, leading to traffic leakage or VLAN hopping risk. After applying these commands, verify both sides of the trunk have matching allowed VLAN lists and the same native VLAN ID to avoid asymmetric behavior. Inter-VLAN routing is required when devices in different VLANs need to communicate. On a Layer 3 switch this is accomplished with Integrated Routing and Bridging interfaces, known as IRB. An IRB interface is a logical interface that holds an IP address and represents the Layer 3 gateway for a specific VLAN. For example, configuring irb.10 with address 192.168.10.1/24 and associating it to VLAN 10 makes that IP the default gateway for devices in VLAN 10. The typical workflow is twofold: create the irb unit and assign the IP, then bind the VLAN's l3-interface to that irb unit using set vlans NAME l3-interface irb. X. A common operational tip is to keep the irb unit number aligned with the VLAN ID to simplify management. A frequent misconception is that an IRB automatically exposes ACLs between VLANs; routing happens by default, so apply firewall filters or policies if you want to restrict traffic between VLANs. In practice, three misconfigurations recur: missing global VLAN definitions, incorrect port mode, and native VLAN mismatches. First, assigning an interface to a VLAN name without creating that VLAN with a vlan-id means the switch has an orphaned assignment; hosts won't be able to reach DHCP or peers in that VLAN. If a host cannot get a DHCP lease, confirm set vlans NAME vlan-id ID exists. Second, configuring an uplink as an access port by mistake isolates the VLAN on that link; this often appears as a whole VLAN unreachable beyond one switch. Check show interfaces terse to verify port-mode. Third, native VLAN mismatches on trunks map untagged frames to different VLANs across the link, producing surprising reachability and a security window. The symptom is traffic arriving in an unexpected VLAN at the remote end. Diagnose this with show interfaces interface-name to confirm native-vlan-id on both sides and align them. Always use show vlans and show route as part of diagnosis. When you find a mismatch, fix configuration and re-verify; sometimes rebooting edge devices is unnecessary if the switch corrects the VLAN mappings immediately.

Here are the three essential concepts to retain. First, VLANs create logical broadcast domains and must be defined with both a name and a vlan-id to operate correctly. Second, 802.1Q trunking carries multiple VLANs over one link; trunks use tags to identify VLAN membership and the native VLAN handles untagged frames, so set it deliberately. Third, inter‑VLAN routing requires IRB interfaces on a Layer 3 switch; bind each VLAN to an IRB with a gateway IP to enable communication between VLANs.
